name: SOFTWARE Hive
os_min: Windows 2000 (present in all NT-based Windows versions)
purpose: Stores machine-wide installed-application data, OS version/build identity, and system-wide autostart (Run/RunOnce) persistence locations that apply to every user of the machine.
key_fields: Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run and \RunOnce — machine-wide autostart command lines (REG_SZ/REG_EXPAND_SZ), run at every user logon
Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\<AppGUID or Name> — DisplayName, DisplayVersion, Publisher, InstallDate, UninstallString, InstallLocation
Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion — ProductName, CurrentBuildNumber, InstallDate, RegisteredOwner
Wow6432Node mirror of the above Run/Uninstall keys, holding 32-bit software entries on 64-bit Windows
normal_baseline: Run/RunOnce entries correspond to known, digitally-signed vendor software (AV agents, GPU tray utilities, cloud-sync clients) launched from Program Files. Uninstall entries match software the organization actually deployed, with plausible InstallDate and Publisher values.
anomalies: A Run or RunOnce value pointing to an executable or script in a user-writable path (%Temp%, %AppData%, Downloads) instead of Program Files.
A Run key value invoking powershell.exe, cmd.exe, mshta.exe, or rundll32.exe with an encoded or heavily obfuscated argument string — a common Registry Run Key persistence pattern.

An Uninstall key entry with no corresponding installed files on disk, or an InstallDate immediately followed by execution of its own UninstallString — suggesting a dropper that installs, runs, and removes its own uninstall metadata to reduce visibility.
An Uninstall entry's Publisher/DisplayName spoofing a well-known, trusted vendor.
anti_forensic_notes: RunOnce values are deleted by Windows automatically once the referenced command has executed, so a RunOnce-based dropper leaves nothing behind in this key after it fires — its absence is expected behavior, not evidence of tampering, and must be correlated with Prefetch or event-log data instead. An attacker may also manually delete a Run value once a longer-term persistence mechanism (e.g. a scheduled task or service) has taken over, leaving only the key's last-write time as a narrow window of evidence.
